HALIMOS (Sea Orache)

Also known as damasonion, also erymon,
also brittanike, also rabdion, also
basilike; the prophets [call it] "Hermes' foundation," like
flesh; also "Osiris's diadem";
also "crown of Pan"; also "sacred oar."
Pythagoras [calls it] anthenoros; the Egyptians
[call it] asphoin; also asontēri; also asello-
ērē; also asaraphē; the Romans call it
labukium; also ampoullakia.

The shrub is a hedge-plant, similar to buckthorn,
though not thorny, and the whole plant
is rather pale, and its leaves,
like those of the olive, are broader, however,
and softer. It grows mostly
in places near the sea, among hedges
and fences, and its leaves are
eaten. A drachma's weight of its root,
drunk with honey-water, helps against
pulled muscles, ruptures, and colic.

ALIKAKKABOS (Winter Cherry / Bladder Cherry)

Also known as dirkaion, also
"mad down," also
doryknion; the Romans [call it]
apollinaris minor, or
herba vaticana; also
ouagem; the Dacians [call it] koikol-;
the Africans [call it] kakkabum.
It has leaves similar to nightshade (strychnos),
though broader. Its
stems, as the plant
grows, become like bladders,
reddish, round, equal
in size to grape berries, and
garland-weavers use them,
weaving them into
garlands.
It has a cooling power,
so its leaves, applied as a poultice,
are good for
erysipelas and creeping sores,
mixed with barley meal.
A marvelous thing besides...

Applied crushed, it treats styes (aigilopia) and headaches,
and relieves burning fever; it is worn for parotid swellings
when crushed and applied as a poultice; and its stalk, too,
[mixed] with egg white, with silver [leaf?], and with rose oil, is good against erysipelas
and [...] against styes, when bound on.

it is beneficial also for earaches [illegible]; it also checks a woman's flux when applied
in wool, so administered. Its fruit, too, is able to purge jaundice,
being diuretic. The herb is also pressed for its juice and dried in the shade, for
storage, against much mustiness.

III.

ARTEMISIA MONOCLONOS, ARTEMISIA
THE OTHER, POLYCLONOS

Some call it toxitis, others Ephesia, others parthenike,
others hypolysson, others Anactoria, others sozousa,
others leia, others leukophryx; the prophets call it "blood of man,"
the Romans ullentia, others serpullum,
others herba regia; the Gauls call it ponem, the Dacians zuzustrum.

It grows for the most part in places near the sea, resembling wormwood,
but larger and broader. One kind of it is vigorous, having broader leaves
along its stems; the other is whiter, with small, fine, strong-smelling flowers,
and it blooms in summer. Sometimes among those growing inland there is
a thinner-fruited plant with a single stalk, bearing a small flower,
pale in color, delicate, which they call artemisia.

Both kinds warm and thin the body. When boiled, they are suitable
for women's sitz-baths, to bring on menstruation, the afterbirth,
and the fetus, and for uterine obstruction and inflammation of the womb,
for breaking up stones, and for retention of urine. The herb, applied as a
plaster in quantity on the lower abdomen, brings on menstruation within a month.
The juice extracted from it, mixed with myrrh and applied as a pessary,
draws out matter from the womb; and when drunk as an enema it promotes
hair growth in the same manner.

APARINE

It has an unripe-grape-like fruit; some call it "philanthropon" (man-loving); some call it "ixos" (bird-lime). It has many long, four-angled, rough stems, with leaves set around at intervals in a circle, like those of madder. The flowers are white; the seed is hard, round, somewhat mottled, with a navel-like depression in the middle. It is also tolerated for use with milk-curdling; shepherds use this plant instead of a strainer for milk, to catch the hairs floating in it. The seed and its juices are drunk, and the leaves when pressed for juice are drunk with wine against persistent inflammations; it is also made into compresses for the ears when mixed as a poultice. The plant, mixed with fat/lard, disperses scrofulous swellings.

ASARON

It is also called wild nard. The prophets called it "limaron"; the Egyptians named it "keras" (?); the Romans [call it] "peressam"; some call it "blachaton"; the Etruscans [call it] "knoumi"; some [call it] "nardourikes"; the Gauls [call it] "baikar"—a plant [used] for garlands, also called "staphylle." It has an earthy [root] with stems that are somewhat rough between the leaves, flowers that are purple, thin, and fragrant; its roots are used like black hellebore, having the smell of cinnamon. It grows in rough and dry places.

The root of this plant, boiled in water, helps with ruptures, spasms, chronic difficulty of breathing, and difficulty of urination. It also helps menstrual disorders and is given after childbirth, administered with wine. Being astringent, it also [helps] in such cases; it is useful for headaches, inflammations, and bruised or swollen conditions, and it strengthens... There is also [another kind] which... [illegible]
[illegible]

CHAMAEDRYS · CHAMAEPITYS · CHAMELAEA ·

Also called chamairōps, also "dryïsken chros,"
also teukrion; the Romans call it tri-
gōminon; the Gauls call it kuerkia,
ereinon. It grows in rough
and rocky places; it is
a small shrub, a cubit high, having
small leaves similar in
shape and form to oak leaves, bitter; its flower is
somewhat purple and small. One should
gather it always when the fruit is forming into clusters.
It has a warming power. When drunk
with water it helps
against spasms, coughs, and an enlarged
spleen; for those with difficulty urinating
and poor digestion it brings on
menstruation and expels embryos;
when drunk together with vinegar it also helps
those with ascites when taken with wine
and applied as a poultice. Ground fine it
can also be formed into pills
as prescribed, and it cleanses
old sores when applied with honey; mixed with olive oil
and applied as a black ointment it stops
discharge from the eyes, and when smeared on
it is warming.

It also helps with hardenings and wounds, and
checks herpetic sores when applied as a poultice with honey.

Also called pitysorueis, also "oroozēn,"
also holokyron, also wild bryonia,
also "anthēnēsin," also

Its leaves, drunk

cure jaundice. It is also given
to those with liver ailments, difficulty urinating,
and kidney trouble, and is suitable
for those with colic. Use it also
for those twisted with pain.
This plant, called "Herakleia" by the

DILL

Some call it pêganon, others aniketon; prophets call it "seed of the dog-headed one," likewise "hairs of the dog-headed one." The Egyptians call it the seed of Hermes... the Romans call it anethum, the Africans sikkiria, the [illegible]... dwellers.

Dill is well known, diuretic, warming, good for the stomach,
good for the stomach, and aids digestion. It should not be taken in excess [illegible] together with the antidotes,
corresponding to the sharp-flavored anise. Its root, boiled, is given with milk
just as [illegible] of dried dill: of the flowering tops and of the fruit
the decoction, when drunk, [relieves] milk disorders, griping pains, and intestinal [troubles,]
being very effective; it stops looseness of the bowels and persistent vomiting,
promotes urination, soothes hiccups, and dulls
the eyesight and the generative faculty when drunk continuously; it is useful [illegible]
useful also is its decoction as a sitz-bath for women's uterine troubles,
and its seed, when applied as a plaster, is said to stop warts (condylomata).

VII.

ASTER ATTICUS (Attic Starwort)

Also called asteriskos, also called asterion, also called boubonion, also called ophthalmos; the Romans [call it] inguinalis, the Dacians rathibida.

It has woody stalks bearing at their tips a purple flower, sometimes pale yellow, like the head of chamomile, surrounded at the top by narrow little leaves; the leaves around the stem are somewhat long and hairy. It is suitable, applied as a poultice, against inflammations of the groin while fresh; and when dried, taken up in the left hand by the sufferer and bound around the groin, it stops the pain.

AMARAKON (Marjoram) [text describes Anthemis/Chamomile]

Also called anthemis, also called leukanthemon, also called parthenion, also called chamaimelon, also called chrysokallis, also called malabathron, also called anthos pedinon; the Romans [call it] "soliseculum," also "millefolia"; the Tuscans "cautam"; the Africans "thamako"; the Gauls "vignita"; the Dacians "douodala."

Its leaves resemble those of coriander, fine and thin; its flowers are white around the edge, with a yellow center; it has a strong smell and a bitter taste.

When the dried material is drunk mixed with honey, like epithymon, it draws out phlegm and bile, and benefits those with asthma and those suffering from melancholy. This herb, apart from its flower, is also beneficial when taken as a drink for asthmatics and those suffering similarly. Its decoction serves as a sitz-bath for a womb that is irritated and inflamed. It is also applied as a poultice, together with its flowers, against erysipelas and other inflammations.

VIII.

AMBROSIA (Botrys)

Some call it botrys, some call it botrys artemisia, the Romans call it "cuprum milvaticum," others call it "apium rusticum," the Egyptians call it "merse." It is a small shrub of great beauty, with leaves like those of the wormwood, growing around the shoot of the stem; they are small, like those of rue, the branches around it bearing much seed, like small clusters, which never wither. It is sown like poppy seeds; its root sends out many shoots in Cappadocia, and it is used for garlands. It has an astringent power over discharges, and when applied as a poultice it is repellent.

WORMWOOD (Apsinthion)

The Egyptians call it "somi," the Romans "apsinthium rusticum," or "the bitter pontic one." The best kind is that growing in Pontus and in Cappadocia, on the mountain Taurus, among the growing plants.

It has a digestive power, and it purifies those suffering within, in the stomach and bowels, driving out bile. It is also diuretic, and when drunk beforehand with a bit of Celtic nard it helps against loss of appetite, and it cures jaundice when drunk continually each day in a cup along with three cyathi [measures], taken also for relief, with honey, against drowning victims and those being strangled, when drunk with wine; and against indigestion and poisoning.

It also helps against the sea-dragon's sting, and for those with quinsy it is applied as an ointment mixed together; for dimness of sight and the surrounding region likewise, and also [for] [illegible]... its decoction is useful for excessive [inflammation], and with honey-wine it serves as a poultice for painful eyes [illegible]... as a remedy it is applied to the hypochondria and the [illegible]... stomach; for those suffering chronic illness it relieves them when combined [illegible]... myrtle oil suits the stomach, and rose oil [illegible]... for dropsical patients mixed likewise with soda and nitre and [illegible].

There is also prepared a wine called "wormwood wine," especially in Italy, around the Propontis and Thrace; and it is used for the purposes already mentioned. People drink it regularly when free of fever, and otherwise always drink a toast of it, believing that in summer it promotes health. It is also thought that when woven in among garments stored in chests, it keeps them from being eaten by moths; and when rubbed on the body together with oil, it prevents gnats from settling on the skin.

Some call it abrotonon, some wormwood (apsinthion), some Herakleion,
some ankona, some apogalon, some merikon,
some choloptoion, some thelyphthorion, some
apsinthiomenon, some prokampylon; the prophets [call it]
nevraphoinikos; some kynanchitis; the Romans
[call it] absinthium ponticum; some call it
lythamnos, a tree-like plant with whitish
small leaves, like wormwood from Seriphos, growing around rocky places,
all of it bears a corymb-like tip,
golden in color, appearing in summer, fragrant,
somewhat bitter in taste. The
Sicilian kind seems to be of this sort, but there is another, coarser
one called "matodes," with thin stems, like
wormwood, growing abundantly in Cappadocia and Galatia,
in the part toward Asia, and also at Hierapolis in
Syria.

The seed of these plants, taken with water
and crushed raw and drunk, helps against orthopnea (difficulty breathing),
ruptures, convulsions, sciatica, difficulty urinating, suppression of
menstruation, and serves as an antidote to deadly
poisons when mixed with wine and applied as a liniment.
Burnt together with olive oil, it drives away pests;
when fumigated and drunk with wine it benefits those in pain;
it specifically treats spider and scorpion bites; it also helps
inflammations of the follicles when boiled with henna oil
and applied as a poultice with bread, it dissolves
and tumors; mixed with honey it is beneficial;
it is also mixed into the preparation of laurel oil.

X.

ARGEMONE

Some call it anthemis, others oinone, others homonoia, others anthos pelinon; the Romans [call it] livornia, others concordialis, others pergalia; the Gauls [call it] korna.
Argemone resembles the wild poppy and the anemone; it differs in having its head somewhat flattened above... [and in] not being purple like the poppy, and it has a round root. Then it exudes a saffron-colored [juice], which [when drawn off like] opium produces... a cleansing effect on argemon (a disease of the eye) and on cataract (nephelion), and it soothes inflammations when the leaves are applied as a poultice.

ANOTHER ARGEMONE

Some call it artemone, others arsela, others sarkokolla; the Romans [call it] argemonia.
This one too resembles the wild poppy in its leaves. It has the property, when fresh and ground fine and applied, of healing inflammations of the eyes and of treating cuts. It is also good for dysentery sufferers when drunk with water; it is adhesive for wounds and inflammations of the sinews. Likewise, applied externally, it is effective for spasms and pains. It is also suitable for those bitten by venomous creatures when taken with wine.

There is a small kind and a large kind. Both are resinous and have diuretic properties; when burned as incense they drive away wild beasts. Their fruit is fragrant, sweet, warming, and diuretic, and is taken for chronic coughs and flatulence. The juniper is called "black"; its leaves are pungent, so that when applied as a poultice or drunk—both the leaves themselves and their juice mixed with wine—they are effective against snakebite. The bark, when burned and applied with water, clears up skin eruptions (leprosy); and the sawdust of the wood, when drunk, is purgative/expels [worms].

There is a wild kind and a cultivated kind, and of the cultivated kind one bears
purple flowers, another whitish, milk-colored ones, another has purple

The root is about the size of an olive, or larger, like a bulb,

leaves and stems, boiled together and so prepared, likewise when
taken as the rest are, bring on menstruation when placed as a
pessary for several months; and when applied as a plaster, they
draw out [disperse] boils.

They grow in shady places and around moist ground. Their stalks are black,
smooth, and glossy; the leaves resemble fern, small and smooth. The underside of
the leaves has lentil-like marks arranged opposite one another along the stalks. They
bear neither stem nor flower; the roots are of no use.

A decoction of the herb can help those suffocating with asthma,
jaundice, and difficulty in urinating. It also breaks up stones, settles the bowels,
and helps those bitten by dogs; it clears phlegm from the stomach, and
brings on the menses — it brings on the menses — and dissolves bile, and helps
with the coughing up of blood. It is also applied as a poultice against the bites of
venomous creatures, and against alopecia (hair loss); it thickens scrofulous swellings,
disperses abscesses, scurf,
and watery discharges, mixed with lye, with ladanum, myrtle oil, and wine,
used generally as a cleansing wash. It also makes roosters and
quails more pugnacious when mixed into their feed.

Of pimpernel there are two kinds, differing from one another in the color of the flower. The one having a blue flower is called the female, while the one with the red flower is called the male. Both are shrubby plants, spreading over the ground, having leaves set upon four-sided stems; the leaves are small and somewhat rounded like those of a small grape-cluster, and the fruit is round. Both kinds are soothing and anti-inflammatory; they help draw out splinters and are useful as a nasal rinse. They relieve toothache if poured into the nostril opposite the aching tooth. They clear away pain when mixed with Attic honey, and help with dimness of sight. Drunk with wine, they help those bitten by vipers, as well as people suffering from dropsy and liver ailments. Some say that the one with the blue flower helps reduce swelling of the spleen, while the red-flowered one, when applied as a poultice, causes irritation.

ANCHOUSA · ANCHOUSA ETERA (Another Anchousa)

XVI.

Some call it katarchousa, others Libyke, others
archibellion, others alkeibiadion, others onoche,
others porphyris, others medousa, others salyx,
others noneas; the Africans call it bouïnesath.
Its leaves resemble those of lettuce,
rough, dark, numerous, spreading out in all directions
from the root, pressed close to the ground, forming a clump.
It has a root about the thickness of a finger, of a
blood-red color, which grows in the ground and
stains the hands when touched. Its flowers are purple.
It grows in rich soil. The root is
astringent and, when mixed with wax and oil,
is applied to heal wounds that occur spontaneously; for
erysipelas it is applied mixed with barley meal, like a plaster, and cures it; it also treats
skin eruptions and leprosy, when ground together with vinegar and applied.
Applied as a pessary, it also brings about abortion.
Its decoction is given
to those suffering from jaundice, kidney disease, and spleen disease,
and to fever patients, mixed with honey-water. Its leaves,
drunk with wine, check diarrhea.
Perfumers also use the root for
fixing the scent of perfumes.

Right margin: "Ankusa etera; anx(ousa) ysa etera"

Others call it alkeibiadion, and the "lip-herb" (cheiles) as some name it.
This plant differs from
the first kind in having
smaller leaves, which are likewise
rough; its stems are thin,
bearing a purple-colored
flower tinged with red. Its root is
red, fairly long, tapering to
a point, having
a blood-like color.
These plants grow in sandy places.
Their power, and that of
the leaves, helps those bitten
by wild animals, especially those bitten
by vipers: eaten,
or drunk, or simply touched
to the wound, and even when chewed
and placed in the mouth
of the creature—if one then spits it out,
it will kill the creature itself.

XVII.

ALYSSON

Some call it aspidion, others apophyllon
trachy, others akkysiton, others
call it alyseton.
It has round leaves similar to [cress];
the fruit is like little shields, double,
in which is the seed. Taken, it checks
fevers accompanied by thirst, and
held in the hand or smelled, it does
the same thing. With honey it clears
away freckles and skin blemishes. It is
also thought to cure the madness
caused by a dog's bite, when pounded
and bound as a poultice on the bite,
and when hung up in a house it is
said to be a protection against the evil
eye for both people and animals.
Tied on with a piece of purple cloth,
it drives away disease in livestock.

...growing on the Taurus mountains in Cappadocia,
after the "trumpet-plants" [salpingia];
the local people call it sandonikon, named

ASCLEPIAS

Some call it kission, others call it kissophyllon ("ivy-leaf"). It sends up long stalks... its leaves are like ivy. It has long, fragrant roots, a heavy-smelling flower, and seed like small dishes (lekiskoi). It grows in the mountains.

Its roots are helpful when drunk in wine for those with griping pains and for those bitten by venomous creatures. The leaves are good for malignant conditions of the womb and of the breasts.

AMMONIACUM

Some call it agasyllon, the plant from which ammoniacum comes; others call it ammoniac incense; others call it krithos; the Romans call it "helioustros," that is, "ammoniaca." This is the gum of a kind of giant fennel (narthex) that grows in the region of Cyrene in Libya.

One should choose the kind that is well-colored, free of wood, frankincense-like, clean in its lumps, and dense, having no impurity, with a root-like smell, and bitter to the taste. Such a lump is called "eryma"; the oily, earthy mass that is mixed in Libya with the ammoniac is the juice of a kind of green giant fennel.

It has a softening, drawing, and dissolving power against hardened swellings; it also purges the bowels somewhat, and it relieves pains of the joints and of sciatica. It helps also those with dropsy, with orthopnea (difficulty breathing while lying flat), and with epilepsy, when licked up with vinegar for those with fluid retention, taken with honey, or sipped with barley-water (ptisane).

It brings on bloody urine; it cleanses white spots (leukomata) on the eyes and roughness of the eyelids; it dissolves these when mixed with vinegar and applied. It relieves enlarged spleens and excessive hardenings, as well as calluses around the joints, when applied as a poultice with honey — it may even cause [something, illegible] to come out. It is also good for bruises and sciatica when rubbed on, mixed with soda (nitron) and vinegar, and with oil of henna (kyprinon elaion).

XXIX.

BETONICA · · BECHION (Coltsfoot)

The Romans call it Vettonica. It has leaves similar to wild dock, but larger and hairier, astringent in taste. It sends up a stem that is not large, with a thin and short root. Its leaves are pressed for juice while fresh, and this is gathered up. It has an astringent property, particularly good for ulcers of the mouth and tonsils, and it is useful for leukomas (white spots on the eye) and wherever astringency is needed.

Bechion — some call it rhechion, others petrine, others peganon, others pithion, others pagonagon, others chamaileuke, others procheton, others arkophyllon, others chamaigeiron; the Egyptians call it saar thra; the Romans call it tussilago, others pharphara; others poustoulago; the Bessi call it asa.

It has leaves like ivy, but larger, growing from the root, whitish on the upper side and greenish on the underside, with many angles. It has a stem about a span long, bearing a pale yellow flower in spring, which it quickly sheds — and at that time the stem too — so that some have supposed the plant to be stemless and flowerless. The root is thin. It grows around meadows and in moist places.

Its leaves, when dried and applied as a poultice, are helpful against erysipelas and all kinds of inflammation. When the root is burned and its smoke inhaled through the open mouth, it cures those troubled by a dry cough; it also dissolves abscesses in the chest. And the root, fumigated [and mixed] in dead wine lees, is drunk boiled in hydromel (honey-water).

BLACK BRYONY: BALLOTE, OR BLACK HOREHOUND

Some call it black vine, some "cheiroma," some "boukranion"; the Romans call it [a corrupted Latin name]; others call it "batanouta," others "vitis alba"; the Africans call it "pegrina." Outwardly it resembles a cultivated vine, but more like a wild one, and its stems grow larger than any such plant, and it also takes hold of trees with its tendrils. The fruit is grape-like, green at first, but black when ripe. The root is black on the outside, but box-wood colored within. In the first sprouting, its shoots are eaten as a vegetable. They are diuretic, beneficial for the spleen, and suited for those who are paralyzed. The root has a power similar to that of the iris for the same purposes. It is also used for beasts of burden whose eyes have become clouded. The leaves, plastered on with wine, are likewise applied to sprains. Applied to burns it [relieves them]; it removes warts, and cleanses dirty ulcers when mixed with honey.

Some call it black horehound, some call it another kind of horehound, some "nophna," some "notianoskelin," some "nosprason," some "notheras," some "nochelis," some "nostelis," some "nophrys," some "gnothouris," some "gnotera" — the Romans call it "appioun," others "meditam," others "oukeraria," others "marrubium canoherinum"; the Egyptians call it "asphos," others "aiski"; the prophets call it "blood of Zion." It sends up square stems, black and hairy, several growing from a single root. GENTIAN

(Latin gloss: Gentiana)

It is also called "kentaurion rhiza" (centaury root), also "Gallic aloe," also "narke," also "cheironion," by the Dardanians "aloeitis," by the Romans "genneus," also "kikenda," also "kouminalis."
It is thought to have been discovered by a certain king of the Illyrians, Gentios, from whom it took its name. Its leaves near the root resemble those of the plantain (arnoglossos), like sorrel; those in the middle of the stem, and especially those near the top, are more divided and smaller. The stem is hollow, about a finger thick, and about two cubits tall, with joints set at intervals and wider gaps between them; it bears leaves and fruit that is light and chaff-like, long, resembling the long birthwort. It grows in high, shady, and well-watered places.

The root has a warming, astringent power. It helps against the bites of venomous creatures when two drachms of it, or of the flower, are drunk together with pepper, rue, and wine; of its juice, about a drachm is given for the same purpose...

GALEOPSIS (also called "dead nettle")

(Latin gloss: Galeopsis, i.e. "dead nettle")

It is also called "galaiobolon," also "galaiphos"; by the Egyptians "aithophi," by the Romans "urtica labonem" [literally "nettle that does not bite"]. It is a small, toothed shrub. In its stem and leaves it resembles the nettle, but its leaves are smoother and have quite a foul smell when rubbed. Its flowers are small and purple. It grows in hedges, along roadsides, and in waste ground.

The leaves and its juice have a dissolving power against skin eruptions, tumors, scrofulous swellings, abscesses, and growths behind the ears. It should be applied as a poultice twice a day with vinegar to make it effective; the poultice and the decoction loosen such growths beneficially. It is thus used for spreading sores, gangrene, and necrosis, applied as a poultice together with salt.

SAVORY (THYMBRA)
Also called "mountain," also "sheep's," also "themitis," also "wild marjoram," also "ageraton." The Romans [call it] cunila rustica, also thymum, also capra rustica. The Egyptians [call it] sekemmen. It grows in rough places, similar to thyme but smaller and more slender, bearing a spike full of greenish flowers. It has the same properties as the aforementioned thyme when taken in the same way, and is also suitable for everyday [dietary] use. The cultivated savory is in every respect weaker than the wild kind, but more pleasant for eating because it lacks the wild kind's excessive sharpness.

THYME (THYMOS)
Also called "thymon," also "white thyme," also "kephalotos," also "epithymis," also "thyrsion." The Dacians [call it] mizela; [another people] call it moutouka; the Romans [call it] thymum; the Egyptians [call it] stephanoi. It is known by everyone as a small shrubby, brushwood-like plant, covered with many narrow little leaves, having small flowering heads that tend toward purple. It grows especially in rocky and poor ground.

It has a warming property. Taken with salt and vinegar, it purges phlegm from the bowels. Its decoction with honey helps those who have difficulty breathing. It expels worms, brings on menstruation, expels the afterbirth and even the embryo [induces abortion], and is diuretic. Mixed with honey and warmed, it is good for bringing up [phlegm] from the chest. It heals fresh swellings and disperses clots of blood. It removes warts and skin growths. Applied with wine and barley meal, it relieves sciatica. It helps those with dim eyesight, and eaten as food it is beneficial; it is also useful for everyday dietary purposes as a seasoning in place of a condiment.

(main text — a passage from Dioscorides' *De Materia Medica* on the medicinal properties of a plant's bark, root, juice, and sap:)

...of the parts, one should proceed thus. The bark of the root has a purging power, and so does the juice; and the sap, drunk with honeyed water, purges both upward and downward. Of the root itself, four obols are given together with three drachms of nettle seed; of the expressed juice, three obols; of the sap, one obol — more than this, if taken, is dangerous. It is suited for purging incorporeal afflictions, chronic pains of the sides, and conditions requiring vomiting; it should be given for such disorders mixed sweetly with food. It also has, after its purging action, a binding power — the sap and the root more than all others of equal strength. Where it is necessary to draw out matter from deep within or to bring about suppuration, this is useful. Hence the juice, when smeared on along with vinegar, and the fresh root rubbed on, thickens the skin; it removes bruises and livid marks — the root or the juice combined with frankincense or wax — but it should not remain more than two hours. If after this one applies a warm seawater fomentation, it also removes freckles when plastered on with honey, and it disperses skin discoloration and reduces swellings. The juice, applied with vinegar, is usefully smeared on; it is also applied to conditions requiring treatment around the lung, the side, the joints, or the feet. It is useful also for drawing conditions outward, for those who are not naturally warm from circumcision. It raises swellings, and it is poured on as a fomentation; it is also kneaded together with fatty substances and placed on the affected area to fill it out.

XL.

"Horse-dock"

Some call it wild dock, the Romans "rumex"-stica; there is a kind of dock, a tall plant growing in low places, in all respects similar, but larger than the smaller dock... When drunk or eaten it relaxes the bowels; applied as a plaster with honey and wax, [the roots], whether fresh or dried, differ in strength. Their roots, whether boiled or raw, when applied as a plaster, heal leprous conditions, lichen, diseased nails; and it is good to first rub the area with vinegar. They also soothe itching; a decoction of them, used as a gargle, relieves toothache when boiled in wine and used as a mouth-rinse. They also disperse scrofulous swellings and parotid tumors when boiled and applied as a plaster with wine; they also help the spleen, applied with vinegar. Some also use the root bound around the neck against scrofula. It also stops a woman's flux when applied crushed. A decoction in wine, when drunk, purges jaundice and expels stones in the bladder; it also brings on the menses, and helps those stung by scorpions.

"Horse-fennel"

Some call it "marathis," others "wild marathon"; the Egyptians call it "sampsou," the prophets "thymarnos," the Romans "feniculum agreste" (wild fennel), others call it "feniculus," others "equinus," others "mium"; the Gauls call it "sistrambo." It is a kind of wild fennel. It bears seed like cachrys (a kind of seed), and has beneath it a fragrant root, which, when drunk, helps those bitten by vipers, breaks up stones, and purges jaundice. A decoction of its leaves, when drunk, brings on milk and purges women after childbirth.

CAUCALIS

Some call it caucon, or wild daucon; others call it [...]tis; Democritus calls it bryss[on]; the Romans call it pede gallinaceum; others call it pede pulli; the Egyptians call it seseli. This too is eaten as a vegetable, both cooked and raw. It is also diuretic when taken fresh.

CALLITRICHON

Some call it polytrichon; others trichomanes; others adianton; others xenopteron; others pteris; others pteron; others arsion; others call the plant korion. The Egyptians call it egyer, the Romans call it cincinalis; others call it tinula; others terra capillus [earth-hair]; others super tiaoum terra. [...] Its leaves resemble coriander, [...] black, strong, [...] lacking stalk. It bears neither stalk nor flower; its root is useless. But the herb itself, when drunk, can help with asthma, jaundice, and difficulty urinating; it also breaks up stones, settles the bowels, helps those bitten by dogs, and helps with discharge from the stomach. It also helps bring on menstruation and stops [bleeding], and it checks the coughing up of blood. When swallowed, it also helps against venomous bites and against alopecia (hair loss), by causing hair to grow thickly; it clears away scrofulous swellings and abscesses, [...] and mixed with myrtle [...] when fumigated and applied to the head, it makes a woman's hair grow thicker. It also makes amber-colored... and makes quails more combative when mixed into their feed. It grows in shaded, damp places, by walls, and near springs.
